rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## Reading culture with words Culture is everything a people make and keep — language, food, festivals, dress, beliefs, manners, buildings — and Nepal is the richest classroom for it on earth: dozens of languages, half a dozen calendars, and every street a living museum where a medieval shrine and a mobile-recharge shop share a wall.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Culture is learned, shared and changing — three adjectives examiners expect.
Compare cultural practices across communities without judging them.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ## The debates, held honestly **"Globalisation is destroying local culture."** Evidence for the prosecution: English crowding mother tongues out of urban playgrounds; festivals compressed into photo opportunities; the same shops, shows and shoes from Kathmandu to Kansas.…  ·  ## The comparison the exam favours | Basis | Folk culture | Popular culture | | --- | --- | --- | | Origin | anonymous, communal, local | named artists, media industries | | Transmission | face to face, generation to generation | streaming, trends, algorithms | | Change rate | slow, stable | fast, seasonal | | Ownership | the community's | copyright's | | Nepal example | deuda, lakhe dance, local melas | film hits,…

rows.text: ## How the exam asks it The **descriptive essay** ("Describe a festival you celebrate") wants one festival, three senses, one sequence, one meaning — depth beats breadth every time. rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. How does culture shape identity? (2 marks) — language, rituals and values give belonging; one example.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Q. Should traditions change with time? (2 marks) — yes, adapt their core values to new contexts; keep the meaning, update the form.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The words that carry the theme Sort the ideas first. **Material culture** is the visible made thing — dress, food, tools, architecture. **Non-material culture** is the carried invisible — language, values, beliefs, etiquette, the sense of what is polite and what is past.…  ·  ## Reading the theme like a writer — the devices of culture writing **Imagery** is the master device, and it is sensory: a festival described by sight alone is a postcard; described by smell (marigolds and incense), sound (deusi songs at the door), taste (sel roti eaten standing up) and touch (rice paste on the forehead), it becomes a place the reader visits.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Culture questions expect the visible/invisible split: artefacts and festivals vs values and worldview — answer with one of each.  ·  Trick 2: For culture-change questions, argue preservation THROUGH change (adaptation) rather than freezing culture — the nuanced stance scores.

rows.text: Q. Should traditions change with time? (2 marks) — yes, adapt their core values to new contexts; keep the meaning, update the form.
